title: "Introduction"
numbered: true
bibliography: refs/thesis.bib
---

Education has been a central element in the functioning of welfare states by promoting the intellectual and cultural development of individuals, enabling access to opportunities and upward social mobility. However, there are well-documented inequalities within the educational system that highlight how students’ background conditions transform and exacerbate initial inequities. In recent years, the commodification of education has given rise to new forms of inequality, creating a scenario in which the expansion of private education competes with the public sector, and in many cases, the ability to pay is synonymous with access to and quality of education [@busemeyer_welfare_2020; @esping-andersen_politics_1985; @lindh_public_2015; @oecd_education_2025]. This phenomenon becomes particularly concerning when we consider that in countries such as Chile, the United States, or Australia, educational provision is primarily private [@castles_oxford_2010; @valenzuela_socioeconomic_2014; @lee_fairness_2024]. These transformations have serious consequences, as market logic and education have come to be viewed as inseparable, leading to the proliferation of various forms of inequality within the education system, such as school segregation and/or the commodification of teaching and learning processes, among others [@piketty_equality_2025].

The processes of commodification, especiallly in education have not only affected institutions but have also had an impact on people’s normative frameworks [@koos_moral_2019; @fourcade_moral_2007]. While one might expect most people to support public provision—especially in countries with greater inequality—various studies have shown that segments of the population support the private alternative and may even endorse the inequalities generated by it [@lindh_public_2015]. This runs counter to general notions of redistribution and social justice, which are rooted in the principles of equality and equity [@walzer_spheres_2010]. In this sense, the private architecture of education has been able to reshape people’s sense of justice. Thus, market justice (proposed by @lane_market_1986) refers to the view that it is fair for access to and the quality of education to be determined by an individual’s or family’s ability to pay. By viewing money as the guiding principle for the provision of education, this concept addresses the legitimization of inequality, making it essential for understanding the cultural and institutional transformations brought about by the commodification of education.

Meritocracy is a fundamental element of educational institutions, but it has also been viewed as a key factor in legitimizing inequalities. Based on effort and talent, meritocracy posits that these two principles should govern the distribution of rewards in society [@sandel_tyranny_2020]. However, various studies have shown that meritocratic beliefs are linked to greater acceptance of inequality, as they attribute success and failure primarily to individual responsibility, functioning as a cultural mechanism that justifies social hierarchies and diminishes perceptions of structural factors that shape individual trajectories [@darnon_belief_2018; @heuer_legitimizing_2020; @mau_inequality_2015; @mijs_unfulfillable_2016; @mijs_paradox_2021]. In this way, meritocratic beliefs serve as auxiliary frames of reference for all individuals, although they have come to shape a narrative of status legitimation to which those in privileged social positions particularly resort.

Although we know there is a link between meritocracy and the legitimization of inequalities, it is necessary to recognize the different types of meritocratic beliefs held by individuals. Various studies have made progress in unraveling this, offering multidimensional perspectives on meritocracy [@zhu_meritocratic_2025; @duru-bellat_whos_2012; @sin_they_2026]. In this context, @castillo_multidimensional_2023 proposes a novel conceptual framework that distinguishes between meritocratic factors—such as effort and talent—and factors of privilege—such as social and economic capital. Furthermore, this framework differentiates between descriptive (perceptions) and ascriptive (preferences) stances, allowing for a better understanding of the multidimensional nature of meritocratic beliefs. However, these meritocratic beliefs take shape and operate differently at the individual and group levels in people’s minds. It is therefore extremely important to account for the heterogeneity and prevalence of each belief configuration observable in society in order to disentangle the web of existing meritocratic belief patterns.

Some studies have sought to understand the diversity of meritocratic beliefs in society [@zhu_meritocratic_2025; @vanhootegem_worlds_2022], their operationalizations of meritocracy do not distinguish between perceptions and preferences, which has important implications for understanding social reality through measurement. There is also research that has already examined the link between meritocracy and market-oriented preferences but without outlining a typology of beliefs that would allow for a detailed examination of the relationships between these two variables [@lindh_public_2015; @castillo_socialization_2024; @castillo_justification_2026]. In light of the foregoing, we pretend to contribute in this line of research based on two new developments: (1) use the framework of preferences and perceptions proposed by @castillo_multidimensional_2023 to better capture the multidimensional nature of meritocratic beliefs configurations. Later, (2) study the link between of meritocratic beliefs and preferences for market justice in education, aiming to observer in what extent meritocracy works as mechanism of inequalities legitimization.
 
The study of the relationship between meritocratic beliefs and the legitimization of inequalities is particularly relevant in Chile, a country that has internalized market-based structures into its social services since the military dictatorship, during which education was one of the sectors that underwent extensive privatization—the foundations of which remain in place to this day [@valenzuela_socioeconomic_2014; @bellei_problema_2025]. Furthermore, the country’s high levels of inequality are striking given its population’s strong adherence to meritocracy, especially with regard to the value placed on effort [@castillo_changes_2025]. Thus, this study aims to contribute to the research on legitimization of inequalities based on two questions: (1) To what extent do meritocratic beliefs influence preferences for market justice in education? (2) How do institutional designs and preferences for market justice in education interact?. This will be answered by analyzing how different configurations of meritocratic beliefs are associated with market justice preferences in education through Latent Class Analysis (LCA). More specifically, we seek to provide a detailed understanding of how the interaction of individual variables can explain the justification of inequality in education. Thus, this research advances our understanding of how people’s normative judgments regarding the legitimization of inequality in education vary, elucidating the factors that shape them. This can provide an assessment of how people normatively perceive the functioning of education, which may serve as a basis for the development of policies aimed at promoting educational justice. 

To adress these issues, we use representative data from the chilean survey EDUMERCO, a study fielded at 2025 to examine attitudes, emotions, and behaviors among adults aged 18 to 75 in relation to inequalities and meritocracy. First, we applied latent class analysis to identify configurations of meritocratic beliefs, and then conduct multinomial logistic regression to examine the relationship between these profiles and preferences for market justice in education, while incorporating sociodemographic and institutional factors.
